snip.s: Medical Microbiology Q&A Guide — MCQ Bank

qs.q: What is the classical clinical finding in acute Chagas disease characterized by unilateral, painless periocular edema?
qs.e: Romana's sign is the classical finding of unilateral, painless periocular edema seen in acute Chagas disease. Winterbottom's sign is found in African trypanosomiasis.

qs.q: What is the primary reason why treatment of Chagas disease with current drugs like nifurtimox and benznidazole has notable limitations?
o: They cannot be administered orally to human patients
They cause permanent blindness in most treated persons
They kill only extracellular forms and not intracellular
They kill only intracellular forms and ignore blood
qs.e: Current drugs used for Chagas disease kill only extracellular forms, leaving intracellular amastigotes largely unaffected. This contributes to the lack of highly effective treatment options.

qs.q: What is the term for the subcutaneous lesion that develops at the inoculation site during acute Chagas disease?
qs.e: A chagoma is a subcutaneous lesion at the inoculation site of Chagas disease. A chancre is associated with African trypanosomiasis inoculation sites.

qs.q: Which organ systems are predominantly targeted during the chronic phase of Chagas disease?
qs.e: Chronic Chagas disease causes inflammatory responses and fibrosis targeting the heart, esophagus, and colon, leading to conditions like megaesophagus and megacolon. The lungs and kidneys are not the primary fibrotic targets listed.

qs.q: Why is the treatment of Chagas disease challenging with current medications like nifurtimox and benznidazole?
o: They are rendered inactive by human serum albumin
They kill only extracellular forms, not intracellular ones
They rapidly cross the blood-brain barrier causing fatal toxicity
They cannot be absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract
qs.e: Current drugs for Chagas disease have the limitation of killing only extracellular forms and failing to target intracellular amastigotes effectively. They are administered orally rather than being blocked by serum albumin.

qs.q: Which preventive measure is specifically emphasized for controlling Chagas disease compared to African trypanosomiasis?
o: Mass screening for Glossina species vectors
Using insect repellents against tsetse flies
Improving housing to reduce vector entry
qs.e: Improving housing conditions and using insecticides target reduviid bugs for Chagas disease prevention. Clearing vegetation and repelling tsetse flies are meant for African trypanosomiasis control.

qs.q: Which infection cycle for Chagas disease involves wild animals such as armadillos and opossums?
qs.e: The sylvatic cycle involves wild animals like armadillos and opossums. The domestic cycle involves humans, while the peridomestic cycle involves domestic animals like dogs and cats.

qs.q: What is the recommended dosing duration for Benznidazole when treating Chagas disease?
qs.e: Benznidazole is given at 5-10 mg/day for 60 days. Nifurtimox has a different dosing schedule involving 4 divided doses daily for up to 120 days.

ai.title: Chagas Disease (American Trypanosomiasis)
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, is a protozoan infection transmitted mainly by triatomine bugs. It has acute and chronic phases, with chronic cardiac and gastrointestinal complications that dominate in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Chagas disease is endemic in Latin America but increasingly seen in migrants worldwide. In low‑resource hospitals, clinicians must rely on clinical clues and basic tests because serology and PCR may be unavailable.
b: Acute phase: often asymptomatic or mild febrile illness
Chronic phase: cardiac arrhythmias, dilated cardiomyopathy, megacolon, megaesophagus

sections.p: Trypanosoma cruzi is a flagellated, intracellular protozoan. It exists as trypomastigotes in the vector’s feces and as amastigotes within host cells.
b: Invades muscle cells, especially cardiac myocytes and smooth muscle of the gut
Resistant to complement; enters cells via lysosome‑dependent pathway

sections.p: The vector is the triatomine (kissing) bug. After a blood meal, infected feces are rubbed into the bite site or mucous membranes. Oral transmission from contaminated food, congenital spread, and transfusion are also important in low‑resource settings.
b: Vector‑borne: bug feces on skin → mucosal or broken‑skin entry
Oral: ingestion of contaminated fruit juice or sugarcane
Congenital: transplacental during acute maternal parasitemia

sections.p: Two clinical phases exist. The acute phase may show a chagoma, Romana’s sign, or nonspecific fever. Chronic infection leads to progressive myocarditis, conduction disease, and gastrointestinal megasyndromes.
b: Acute myocarditis: chest pain, tachycardia, elevated troponin
Chronic cardiomyopathy: LV dilation, heart failure, arrhythmias

sections.p: If serology or PCR is unavailable, rely on ECG/ECHO changes plus epidemiologic exposure to make a presumptive diagnosis.

t.b: Detects circulating trypomastigotes; a positive result confirms acute infection

t.a: Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) for T. cruzi antibodies
t.b: Answers if chronic infection is present; a positive result supports chronic disease
Shows conduction blocks, arrhythmias, or low voltage; suggests cardiac involvement
Assesses ventricular size and function; identifies dilated cardiomyopathy

sections.p: Vector control (insecticide spraying, housing improvement) and screening of blood donors are public‑health priorities.
b: Benznidazole: preferred because of better tolerance; avoid in severe hepatic disease
Heart failure: ACE‑inhibitor, diuretic, beta‑blocker as per standard guidelines
Arrhythmias: amiodarone or implantable cardioverter‑defibrillator if available

sections.p: Focus on the clinical transition from acute to chronic disease, the characteristic cardiac findings, and the limited diagnostic tools in low‑resource settings.
b: Romana’s sign (unilateral periorbital swelling) points to vector entry through conjunctiva
Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy often presents with a right‑bundle‑branch block on ECG
Megacolon in a migrant from endemic area with chronic constipation suggests Chagas

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden cardiac arrest, severe heart failure (NYHA IV), or life‑threatening arrhythmias

faq.q: Why is benznidazole preferred over nifurtimox?
faq.a: Benznidazole has higher cure rates in acute infection and fewer neurologic side effects.

faq.q: Can Chagas disease be transmitted by blood transfusion?
faq.a: Yes; screening donors in endemic areas is essential.
Swelling of the eyelid on the side of the bite, caused by conjunctival entry of the parasite.

exam: A 35‑year‑old migrant from Bolivia presents with new‑onset heart failure; what is the most likely underlying cause and which test confirms it? — Look for chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy; confirm with T. cruzi antibody test or ECG changes.
A patient has fever, periorbital swelling, and a chagoma after a night in a rural house; what is the next best step? — Treat acute infection with benznidazole; start before serology returns.

How does the ECG pattern in chronic Chagas differ from typical ischemic heart disease? — Chagas often shows right‑bundle‑branch block and left‑anterior‑ fascicular block without reciprocal ST changes.
Why is nifurtimox avoided in a patient with severe depression? — Nifurtimox can cause neuropsychiatric toxicity, worsening depression.

In a low‑resource clinic without serology, how would you diagnose chronic Chagas in a patient with megacolon? — Combine epidemiologic exposure, chronic constipation, and characteristic radiographic dilation; treat presumptively.
What public‑health measures reduce new Chagas cases in endemic regions? — Vector control, housing improvement, and blood‑bank screening.
A pregnant woman from an endemic area is seropositive; what management is recommended for the newborn? — Monitor infant with PCR or serology at 9 months; treat if positive.
Which cardiac complication of Chagas carries the highest mortality and how is it managed? — Sudden ventricular arrhythmia; manage with anti‑arrhythmic drugs and consider ICD implantation.
